chose: dedupe on a stored `metric` label, one OPEN conjecture per label at a time — and a RESOLVED one keeps the label quiet until the value moves a further threshold-width past the value that was resolved
over: dedupe on the content-hash id (the existing mechanism) — it cannot work, because the value is IN the observation text and changes every run, so ten runs mint ten ids and ten open questions

dedupe on label forever, so a label that ever produced a conjecture never produces another — that trades the spam generator for a silence generator: the second, larger excursion is exactly the one worth asking about
dedupe on a time window (one conjecture per label per day/run) — a clock is not the identity of a question, and it re-opens on a schedule rather than on new evidence
because: the identity of the QUESTION is 'why is <label> outside its band', which is stable across runs while the number is not. So the dedupe key must be the label, not the measurement. The resolved-state rule falls out of the same reading: a resolution answers the excursion it was written against, so an excursion that has moved a further threshold-width beyond the resolved value is a DIFFERENT question and deserves to be asked. Requires storing `value` on the record, which the journal wanted anyway

chose: return-to-band NEVER auto-resolves; it prints the open conjecture's id and the exact `coherence resolved` line instead
over: auto-resolve when the metric comes back inside its band
auto-retract the conjecture on return, on the theory that the observation stopped holding
because: a resolution's `because` field is what the discriminating test SHOWED. A number wandering back shows nothing about the cause, so an auto-resolution would have to write a false claim ('it came back') into the one field that carries evidence. The failure is also silent and asymmetric: it deletes an entry from `decisions --open` — the single list this feature exists to populate — and deletes it precisely in the case where nobody looked. And it closes the most interesting questions preferentially: a metric that left its band and returned has usually done something stranger (a transient, an accidental revert, a non-monotonicity) than one that stayed out. Silence is the other failure, so the return IS reported — on stdout, as evidence a human may resolve WITH, never as the resolution

chose: an explained move (--why) is written as a conjecture PLUS its resolution — born answered — and when a conjecture is already open for that label the --why RESOLVES it
over: a plain `decision` record: it would land in Standing with an empty `over`, reporting a metric move as a settled choice
a new record kind `observation`, with its own render section
writing nothing at all when --why is present, on the grounds that the source file already holds the explanation
because: the journal already has exactly the shape 'a notable move, and what accounted for it': a conjecture with a resolution pointing at it. Reusing it means an explained-immediately move and an explained-three-weeks-later move render identically, which is correct — the reader cares what the answer is, not how fast it arrived. It also needs no new kind, no new render branch, and no change to resolve(). The open-conjecture case is the loop closing itself: coherence asked the question, the project filled in the `why` field its own table already has, and the next harness run carries that answer back in

chose: match the consuming table's `Math.abs(delta) >= threshold` byte-for-byte, float wobble included, instead of adding an epsilon or a relative tolerance
over: an epsilon around the threshold, so a move of 'exactly one band' in decimal counts as notable
a relative comparison (|delta| / |baseline|) so the bar scales with the metric
because: measured while writing the test: 0.15 - 0.14 is 0.00999999999999998, so a decimal move that LOOKS like exactly one band is under a 0.010 threshold and the row prints as not-moved. Any correction here would be a correction coherence applied and planetizer did not, and the two halves would then disagree exactly at the boundary — the one place a disagreement is invisible, because it is the case nobody eyeballs. Being wrong the SAME way is worth more than being right alone. The relative form is worse still: notableDelta is an ABSOLUTE physical quantity (o2's 0.01 is a tenth of the O2_ANIMAL_MIN..O2_FIRE_THRESHOLD band), and dividing it by the baseline would silently re-scale a bar the project derived from the manual. Pinned in test/observed.test.ts as a fact, not routed around

chose: negative controls on BOTH new behaviours: the label dedupe and the refusal to auto-resolve
over: one negative control on the dedupe only, since it is the load-bearing one
because: ran two. (2) RETURN-TO-BAND: made a return inside the band resolve the open conjecture with because='the metric returned to its band'. Restored byte-identical against a saved copy both times (diff clean), 356/356 after. chose: usage errors exit 2, against the brief's letter of 'exit code 0 always'
over: exit 0 unconditionally, including on --value banana or a missing --threshold, as literally specified
because: the brief's 'exit 0 always. A malformed invocation is not an observation. Exiting 0 on a typo'd flag would make the harness stop asking questions silently, which is this repo's own named defect ('a command that exits 0 and does nothing, which is the defect this harness exists to hunt', cli.ts resolved branch) and the same failure as the negative control whose regex never matched. --threshold in particular has no default and must not acquire one: the bar is domain knowledge that lives on the project's side of the seam, so a missing one is a missing BAR, not a zero

chose: an advisory finding's identity is its SUBJECT — the addressable thing a reader would go look at — stored in a new `finding` field and namespaced by the advisory that formed it

reuse observed's `metric` field with a namespaced value

Line numbers are navigation, not structure (cli.ts already normalizes them out of graph.json for exactly this reason), so the site key is file#kind:name with the line dropped. `metric` was rejected as the carrier because its docblock says it holds a tracked metric and a raise has no number — a field whose name lies is the next reader's trap.

chose: the volume guard is THREE layers: --raise opt-in, the advisory's own reporting floor, and a hard per-run cap that announces what it withheld
over: opt-in alone
the reporting floor alone
a cap alone
because: each layer fails differently and the failure modes do not overlap. Opt-in stops a pre-commit verify from silently writing to the journal (planetizer runs verify in its hook). The floor stops `redundancy --all` — which drops minScore to 0 — from raising the tail it exists to expose; raising always uses the DEFAULT floor, never --all's. The cap bounds the FIRST run on a repo with a long list, which is the case that kills the mechanism on contact. Silence about the withheld remainder was rejected outright: a truncated list that looks complete is the defect this harness hunts.

chose: dismissal is a new record KIND that supersedes a conjecture, ranked below retraction and below resolution
over: a flag on the resolution record (`resolved --dismiss`)
a `dismissed` list in config, keyed on the finding
deleting the conjecture line
because: "we answered this" and "we decided not to ask" are different facts and the render has to be able to lead with the first. A flag on a resolution would put a dismissal in the Resolved section, where a reader counts it as an answer — the same confusion `resolve()` already refuses between a conjecture and a decision. A config list would be an EDIT; the journal is append-only and a dismissal that rewrites history is indistinguishable from one that was always right. Precedence: retraction (the observation was never real) beats resolution (we know the answer) beats dismissal (we chose not to ask), because showing a dismissal for a question that has an answer on file HIDES the answer.

chose: the per-run cap is spent ROUND-ROBIN across advisories, not in strict priority order
over: strict priority (never-red, then warned-kind, then refutation) with the starvation made visible in the withheld line
because: the first dogfood run refuted the priority design on the spot: planetizer @HEAD offered 14 never-red findings and 3 warned-kind, and the withheld line read `never-red 9 · warned-kind 3` — every warned-kind question queued behind twelve others, on the one repo whose config explicitly declares that kind the suspect one. Visible starvation is still starvation. Round-robin bounds it at one round per advisory and the caller's ranking still orders within a round.

chose: the COMMAND registry lives in a new src/commands.ts, not in src/cli.ts beside the dispatch
over: src/cli.ts, adjacent to the if/else dispatch it describes
src/render-commands.ts, matching the render-* naming convention
because: cli.ts EXECUTES at import time (top-level process.argv dispatch and process.exit), so a test that imports a registry living there would run the CLI and exit(2) — the totality oracle is the whole point of the exercise and it must be able to import the source of truth. render-* was rejected because the registry and its two derived spellings are the reason the file exists; splitting them buys an import hop and nothing else.

chose: a registry + a totality oracle that reads the LIVE dispatch out of cli.ts's AST, with the banner and the README index derived
over: a Record<name, handler> dispatch table that deletes the correspondence outright instead of checking it
a hand-written expected-command list in the test
because: the handler table is the strongest form and should happen eventually, but cli.ts's dispatch is 350 lines of early exits, shared locals and per-command usage errors: rewriting it to land a documentation fix trades a checked correspondence for an unchecked rewrite. A hand-written expected list was rejected outright — it would be a FOURTH spelling of the same domain and would drift exactly like the other three. The oracle reads the AST rather than a regex because a regex also matches cmd === "x" inside a comment, and an oracle a code comment can fool is not one.

chose: the derived README index is a BULLET LIST, and the scaffold entry's usage reads <kind> rather than spelling its four kinds
over: a markdown table, which reads better as an index
carrying <boundary|component|invariant|parity> through from the old banner line
because: redundancy reads the first column of every markdown table as an enumerated domain, so a generated table hands it a fresh README-vs-dispatch pair — trading the finding this change removes for an identical one, which fixes nothing. Same reasoning one level down for the scaffold kinds: a DERIVED index propagates whatever the registry spells, and README already spelled those four in prose, so carrying them added a pair. Measured: with <kind>, redundancy goes 42 pairs to 37 with ZERO added; carrying the alternation added one new sub-floor pair.

chose: docs --check treats an absent README fence pair as NOT OWNED (green), while claude --check reds on absent markers
over: one uniform rule — red on missing markers for both owned blocks
silently skipping either way, with no output
because: docs runs in every consuming project, and a gate that fails on a file the project never opted into is a gate that gets switched off wholesale; claude is opt-in per invocation, so there a missing marker pair genuinely means the file failed to get wired up. The skip is not SILENT though — the write path prints the marker pair to paste, because a command that exits 0 having done nothing is the exact defect this harness exists to catch.

chose: measured the redundancy acceptance test from an isolated git worktree at b498b7d with node_modules symlinked in
over: git stash push --include-untracked around the measurement
git checkout <ref> -- . to revert in place
because: checkout -- . does NOT delete files absent from the ref, so the baseline ran with b498b7d's cli.ts AND the new src/commands.ts both present and reported a fabricated 39-pair baseline with pairs that exist in neither tree. The stash form is sound but silently mixes measurement with mutation of the tree under test. A worktree cannot be contaminated by the working copy — and it fails LOUDLY rather than quietly when node_modules is missing, which is how the first contaminated number got caught.

chose: the difference was intended but undeclared for the one visible token, on top of a correspondence that was genuinely unmaintained — and the fix taken was the tier-1 one the discriminator names: derive, so the pair stops existing
because: Put side by side as instructed. The single token the detector saw (only in the dispatch: `resolve`) was NOT drift — it is a legitimate alias, and a banner listing it as a command of its own would be wrong. So candidate 3 won on that token: overlapping-but-deliberately-different domains that nobody had written down. But the correspondence itself had also genuinely drifted (banner 29 vs dispatch 30; v0.14.0's only merge conflict was two branches hand-editing the banner literal), so candidate 2 held for the pair's history. Both are now moot: src/commands.ts is the single declarative home, the banner is .map()ped from it, README's index is spliced from it, and aliases are a first-class field so `resolve` is dispatched without being advertised — the thing nobody had written down is now the thing that IS written down. Measured from an isolated worktree at b498b7d: redundancy goes 42 candidate pairs to 37, five removed and zero added, and this pair is gone from the pair set entirely rather than demoted below the floor. THE INSTRUMENT WAS NOT WRONG — the highest-prior candidate lost. redundancy reported this pair on every run since it shipped and was correct every time.

chose: derived the ENTIRE usage banner from the registry — grouped per-command lines with usage and summary — not just the <a|b|c> alternation the brief named
over: deriving only the alternation line and keeping the 25 hand-written curated help lines below it
because: the brief asked for the alternation literal to go away, and stopping there would have left 25 lines that name commands and drift silently. Those lines were also a CURATED SUBSET: they detailed the journal verbs and flags while omitting graph, overview, docs, claude, onboard, decompose, drift and phrasebook entirely, so the help screen was incomplete in exactly the way the README was. Deriving all 31 costs ~13 lines of banner and buys completeness. What was deliberately NOT absorbed: the per-command usage ERRORS (decide/conjecture/observed/dismiss print their own multi-paragraph help on bad input) — those stay hand-written, because a command's own error is the right place for its domain and its nuance, and the banner is an index.

chose: absorbed the README's pure one-liner command bullets into the registry's summary field, and kept every bullet carrying a WHY as authored detail below the fence
over: keeping all the authored bullets and letting the derived index duplicate the one-liners
deleting the whole ## Commands prose and generating the entire section
because: a bullet that only restates name-plus-one-line IS the list, not detail about it, so leaving it beside the derived index is the same two-spellings defect one level down — a reader seeing both and finding them different has no way to tell which is authoritative. chose: the hook reads the parent session's cwd, not the subagent's working repo
because: Ran the discriminator. planetizer's journal — the parent session's cwd — reports exactly 5 OPEN CONJECTURE(S), and `cat .coherence/decisions/*.jsonl | grep -vc '"kind":"session"'` there returns exactly 74. Both of the hook's numbers match planetizer to the digit, so it is reading that repo's journal, not coherence's. Not a stale cache: the count was correct for the repo it was actually looking at, both times. Not an instrument defect either — stopReport calls the same readJournal + resolve that renderJournal calls, and computes correctly over whatever cwd it is handed. THE CONSEQUENCE IS A WORDING BUG, and it is the kind this project cares about: the message says OPEN CONJECTURE(S) IN THIS REPO, and for a subagent working in a different repo than its parent, 'this repo' names the wrong one — so the nag points at questions the agent cannot see and stays silent about the ones it just created. My own decisions went to coherence's journal correctly (npx coherence ran from the coherence directory), so only the REPORT crossed repos, never the writes.

Reproduction: run any subagent whose cwd differs from its parent's; the stop report's counts describe the parent's journal.
